subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the function of tRNA during translation?
options: To unwind the DNA double helix
To bring specific amino acids to the ribosome according to its anticodon
To carry the genetic code from the nucleus to the ribosome
questions.explain: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and pairs its anticodon with the complementary mRNA codon.

questions.q: After 3 complete cycles of PCR starting from one double-stranded DNA molecule, the number of DNA molecules produced is:
questions.explain: PCR doubles the DNA each cycle, so after 3 cycles there are 2 cubed = 8 molecules.

questions.q: Which feature of the genetic code means each base is part of only one triplet?
questions.explain: In a non-overlapping code each base is read only once, belonging to a single codon.

questions.q: What is the role of DNA helicase during replication?
options: Joining adjacent nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds
Breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases to unwind the double helix
Adding free nucleotides in a 3' to 5' direction
Proofreading newly added bases for errors
questions.explain: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, separating the two strands of the double helix.

questions.q: In prokaryotes, unlike eukaryotes, mRNA does not require splicing because:
questions.explain: Prokaryotic genes generally lack introns, so the mRNA is functional without splicing.

questions.q: A nonsense mutation produces a premature stop codon. The most likely effect on the polypeptide is that it will be:
questions.explain: A premature stop codon ends translation early, producing a shortened, usually non-functional protein.

questions.q: Epigenetic modifications differ from mutations because they:
options: Change the sequence of DNA bases
Affect gene expression without changing the DNA base sequence
questions.explain: Epigenetic changes (e.g. methylation, acetylation) alter gene expression without altering the underlying base sequence.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative rather than conservative because experiments showed that after one round of replication in heavy then light isotopes, all DNA was:
options: A mixture of fully heavy and fully light molecules
Of intermediate density (one heavy strand, one light strand)
questions.explain: Meselson and Stahl found a single intermediate-density band after one generation, supporting semi-conservative replication.

questions.q: In PCR, the temperature is raised to around 95 degrees C in order to:
options: Separate the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
questions.explain: Denaturation at ~95 degrees C breaks the hydrogen bonds, separating the DNA into single strands.

questions.q: Reverse transcriptase is used in genetic engineering to:
options: Cut DNA at specific recognition sites
Synthesise complementary DNA (cDNA) from an mRNA template
questions.explain: Reverse transcriptase makes single-stranded cDNA from mRNA, a useful intron-free copy of a gene.

questions.q: The site of translation in a eukaryotic cell is the:
questions.explain: Translation occurs at ribosomes, where mRNA codons are read to assemble a polypeptide.

questions.q: During transcription, which enzyme joins RNA nucleotides together to form pre-mRNA?
questions.explain: RNA polymerase catalyses the formation of phosphodiester bonds between RNA nucleotides during transcription.

questions.q: Oestrogen affects gene expression by:
options: Binding to DNA polymerase to speed up replication
Binding to a receptor to form a transcription factor complex that switches on target genes
Methylating cytosine bases to silence genes
questions.explain: Oestrogen binds its receptor, and the complex acts as a transcription factor that initiates transcription of target genes.

questions.q: In PCR, the function of the primers is to:
options: Cut the DNA at specific sites
Provide a starting point with a free 3'-OH for DNA polymerase
questions.explain: Primers anneal to the template and provide the free 3' end that DNA polymerase needs to begin synthesis.

questions.q: Increased methylation of DNA in a gene's promoter region typically results in:
options: A change in the DNA base sequence
questions.explain: Promoter methylation usually prevents transcription factor binding, inhibiting transcription without altering the base sequence.

questions.q: In semi-conservative replication, each new DNA molecule consists of:
options: One original strand and one new strand
Fragments of both original strands recombined
questions.explain: Each daughter molecule conserves one parental strand which acts as a template for one newly synthesised strand.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, splicing of pre-mRNA involves:
options: Addition of a poly-A tail only
Removal of introns and joining of exons
Removal of exons and joining of introns
questions.explain: Splicing removes the non-coding introns and joins the exons together to produce mature mRNA.

questions.q: Activated nucleotides used in DNA replication carry two extra phosphate groups. The breaking of these bonds:
options: Removes errors from the new strand
Releases energy that drives the condensation reaction joining nucleotides
questions.explain: Hydrolysis of the two additional phosphates releases energy that powers phosphodiester bond formation.

questions.q: Decreased acetylation of histones (deacetylation) tends to:
options: Make chromatin more condensed and decrease transcription
questions.explain: Histone deacetylation increases positive charge, tightening DNA-histone binding and condensing chromatin to reduce transcription.

questions.q: Restriction endonucleases that leave 'sticky ends' are useful in recombinant DNA technology because:
options: They permanently join DNA without ligase
The single-stranded overhangs allow complementary fragments to anneal before ligation
They cut DNA into blunt fragments only
questions.explain: Sticky ends are short single-stranded overhangs that base-pair with complementary ends, allowing DNA ligase to join the fragments.

questions.q: During translation, the bond formed between adjacent amino acids on the ribosome is a:
questions.explain: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in a condensation reaction catalysed at the ribosome.

questions.q: During gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments, the fragments move towards the anode (positive electrode) because:
options: Larger fragments are repelled by the gel
DNA carries an overall positive charge
The phosphate groups give DNA an overall negative charge
questions.explain: The phosphate backbone gives DNA a net negative charge, so fragments migrate towards the positive anode.

questions.q: How many different codons are possible using a triplet code of four bases?
questions.explain: With four bases in groups of three, 4 cubed = 64 possible codons.

questions.q: A tRNA anticodon is 5'-UAC-3'. The mRNA codon it pairs with is:
questions.explain: Antiparallel complementary base pairing of anticodon 5'-UAC-3' gives codon 5'-GUA-3'.

questions.q: A substitution mutation in a coding region may have no effect on the polypeptide produced. This is most likely because:
options: The degenerate nature of the code means the new codon may still code for the same amino acid
The mutation occurs in an intron only
questions.explain: Owing to degeneracy, an altered codon can still specify the same amino acid (a synonymous/silent mutation).

questions.q: Which type of mutation is most likely to alter every amino acid downstream of the mutation site?
options: A deletion of a single base
A substitution at the third base of a codon
questions.explain: A single-base deletion shifts the reading frame, changing all subsequent codons (a frameshift).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the genetic code?
questions.explain: The code is non-overlapping, not overlapping; each base is read as part of only one codon.

questions.q: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end of a strand. This explains why:
options: Helicase is required to join the fragments
The leading strand is synthesised in fragments
The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously as Okazaki fragments
questions.explain: Because synthesis must run 5' to 3', the antiparallel lagging strand is built discontinuously as Okazaki fragments later joined by ligase.

questions.q: DNA ligase is required in recombinant DNA technology to:
options: Form phosphodiester bonds joining the DNA fragment into the vector
questions.explain: Ligase catalyses phosphodiester bond formation, sealing the inserted DNA into the vector backbone.

questions.q: On the leading strand during DNA replication, synthesis is:
options: Continuous, following the replication fork in a 5' to 3' direction
questions.explain: The leading strand template runs 3' to 5' towards the fork, so DNA polymerase synthesises it continuously 5' to 3'.
